To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
high affinity CD4 TCRs are more effective in anti-tumor immunity than low affinity TCRs.
CD4+ cells expressing high-affinity T cells have improved anti-tumor activity in vivo compared to wild-type affinity.
CD4+ helper cells expressing a high affinity TCR have improved anti-tumor properties compared to wild-type CD4+ TCRs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design and engineering of TCRs with improved affinity for tumor antigens and the development of T cells expressing these engineered TCRs.
the development of TCR gene therapy for cancer treatment and we are currently testing the high-affinity T cells in a Phase I clinical trial at the National Cancer Institute.
the design and engineering of TCRs for adoptive cell therapy of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the nanomolar affinity is better than the micromolar affinity for TCRs in tumor targeting.
nanomolar affinity of TCRs expressed on CD4+ T cell can be advantageous for adoptive cell transfer therapy for cancer.
the affinity of the T cell receptor is an important factor to consider when designing adoptive T cell therapies for cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nanomolar TCRs in T cells have improved anti-tumor effect than the micromolar TCRs.
high-affinity T cells have improved tumor targeting and anti-tumor efficacy.
high-affinity T cells are superior to low-affinity T cells for adoptive immunotherapy of cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TCR affinity should be carefully considered for adoptive cell therapy, especially for CD4+ T-cell therapy.
high affinity TCRs are not necessarily better than lower affinity ones.
the affinity of the T-cell receptor (TCR) is important when considering TCR gene transfer into CD4 T cells.
